cim_eredeti: Why Districts Should Introduce AI to Teachers and Staff Before Students
szoveg_eredeti:
At the Sweet Home Central School District, outside Buffalo, N.Y., laying out a single after-school bus run used to take the transportation office about six hours, and a student who wanted a seat had to sign up two weeks ahead. Then the district built its own artificial intelligence routing tool. “We’ve reduced it into minutes,” Superintendent Mike Ginestre told Education Week in a recent interview. The tool belongs to the transportation office. No student uses it.

That bus run probably deserves more attention than most of what we argue about around AI in education. Since 2022, the national conversation about AI in schools has started with students: when they should have it, in which grades, with what guardrails and processes to catch cheating. Districts have worked hard on those questions, and they are important to consider.

However, we may be asking them in the wrong order. What if the first question was when and how the central office, school administrators and teachers could use AI on their own work, so they can spend more of their time, energy and talent on students and parents? I spent five years leading IT for a network of Catholic schools, and I know how much of a school’s day never reaches a student.

Click the banner below to find tools to enable AI innovation at your district.

The student question is the hardest one in the building, and the evidence dictates that we take it seriously. When Hamsa Bastani, a researcher and Wharton School associate professor, and colleagues took AI away from nearly a thousand high school math students, those who had practiced with a standard chatbot scored 17% lower than students who never used it, while a version built to protect learning largely prevented the loss. The model was the same — the design decided the result. A district that hurries that design can set its students back.

The adult question is a different kind of problem. A bus route or a state report has a right answer that a person can check. The work repeats, it follows rules, and somebody in the office already knows what a good result looks like. There is also a great deal of it. “We have so many reports to file, and we do all of this work by hand,” Ginestre told Education Week. And schools are short of people to do it. Going into the 2024–25 school year, 69% of public schools reported difficulty filling at least one nonteaching position.

I came to this view by observing a superintendent. I lead TechBuffalo, a nonprofit that works with Western New York’s schools and employers to build the region’s talent, with a large focus on tech talent. Technology executives who advise us recently met to hear Mike Sullivan, co-founder of OneDigital, a 6,000-person firm that has undergone an AI transformation, adding digital coworkers. Superintendent Ginestre sat in the room as my guest.

After hearing how AI transformed this massive enterprise business, Ginestre had a light bulb moment, and Sweet Home opted in. Alongside business leaders from that room, the district will now be piloting AI coworkers with TechBuffalo and Radial Ventures, a Buffalo-based venture studio. An AI coworker is hired the way a person is, with a job description, a human supervisor and a performance review. It takes the reducible work that buries a central office — the reports and the data entry — and leaves people the judgment, the relationships and every decision about a child. Nobody goes into education to route buses or file superfluous reports. Ginestre wants the hours back so he can “get out to more buildings, see more people, do more human interactions and build relationships.”

DISCOVER: AI-ready classrooms must prioritize safety.

In Buffalo, teachers started AI journeys within their own work too. From April to June 2026, the K–12 teachers in our Innovation Fellowship sat inside Buffalo startups, in the team meetings where AI is changing daily work.

Then the teachers built, and this is where the Fellowship turned. Most AI reaches a teacher inside a product built first with the student in mind, with the model set behind the safeguards a student needs. In our program, we gave each Fellow direct access to a frontier model, the most capable kind there is, to use on their own work. They were stunned. A teacher who had never written code described a problem from his own classroom in plain sentences and watched the first version of an app appear.

Each Fellow learned to make an app and an AI agent and pointed the agent at the repetitive work in their own week. Nothing else in the program came close, and the excitement carried through the summer as those agents and apps came to life.

The gap the Fellows discovered is also a purchasing question. A product built first for students may be underserving the faculty. Teachers across the country report what the right tool is worth. In a 2025 Gallup survey of 2,232 public school teachers, those who used AI at least weekly estimated it saved them 5.9 hours a week, which adds up to six weeks over a school year. In Gallup’s 2026 survey, 82% of teachers said they receive no formal guidance on how to apply AI to their work. Imagine the time reinvested in students if training were formalized and the AI model were truly matched to the need. Before you sign for the next product, I’d encourage you to ask the vendor to show it doing a teacher’s work as well as a student’s.

READ MORE: Back office and IT staff use AI to boost efficiency.

An adults-first model is exactly how a district gets ready for students. Our Fellows did not bring AI to a classroom until they had used it on their own work and designed the student experience alongside expert faculty at the University at Buffalo Graduate School of Education. Students came last, and they came to teachers who had used the technology for months and were prepared to introduce AI to students in a meaningful way.

“We got into teaching to be with students and to partner with parents,” Ginestre said. Go back to the six hours in his transportation office. Your administrators — and likely your teachers — have a job like that one, and the people who have to do it can name it without thinking.
